correctness.rationale: For the unnormalized 16-DFT the squared lower gain on each fixed C is the least Gram eigenvalue. An odd multiplier on rows permutes supports, and translation changes only unit phases on columns, so the minimum over C is affine-invariant. Repeated row classes modulo four duplicate rows on C={0,4,8,12}; the converse is the prime-power full-spark theorem (balanced residues at each divisor of 16, implied here by one representative of each class modulo 4). The independently written exact reproduction at /workspace/branches/c64e8ab6-aba3-4c76-900e-19f789cfd1a9/reproduce.py exhausts all 1,820 row sets and verifies the 256 balanced sets decompose into disjoint affine orbits of sizes 64,128,64. Its reproduction.log lines 2–3 give negative determinants of 1000G−I on one support for each competing orbit, implying a strictly subthreshold eigenvalue. Line 4 records strict positive signs for every one of 7,280 leading principal minors for the last orbit representative: exhaustive enumeration of 1,820 supports, recursive determinants in Z[x]/(x^8+1) and integer radical enclosures. Sylvester's criterion gives a strictly superthreshold least eigenvalue at every support, hence also for the finite minimum. The determinant digest matches the frozen exact certificate; its supplied code and optional floating-point diagnostic were inspected but not executed. This proves the affine optimizer class and the 64/192/1564 split. Neither the spectral condition-number ratio nor blind unknown-support identifiability with four samples follows; the result compares the gain conditional on each frequency support.

value.rationale: The finite case compares a motivated stability invariant in a cyclic Fourier inverse problem, not a convenient isolated minor. It distinguishes all fixed-size designs by a strict uniform bound and shows that, among universally invertible four-sample designs, the consecutive baseline is not optimal. The quantitative comparison is useful for this order even without an exact expression for the optimal eigenvalue or an all-orders theorem.
